messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Samir is a 41-year-old single man who works as a construction worker. He grew up in a household where, between the ages of seven and ten, he repeatedly witnessed his father assaulting his mother. The memories of those nights are fragmented and strange to him now. Some moments are extremely clear—he can see the exact pattern of the living room rug, the way his mother’s hand gripped the doorframe—while other stretches are completely blank, as if someone erased parts of the film. When he tries to deliberately remember what happened, he finds it difficult to access the memory; the whole thing feels slippery, like trying to hold water. Yet when something reminds him, the memory comes back like a photograph, unbidden and vivid, as if he is looking at a still image in his mind.

In the weeks and months after the violence ended—his father eventually left—Samir began to notice that certain situations would pull those images to the surface. Confrontations, even small ones, were the worst. A coworker raising his voice over a misplaced tool would make Samir’s chest tighten, and suddenly he would see his mother’s face, the way she looked just before the first blow. The memory would surge up, and Samir would find himself drifting off into a world of his own, a fantasy escape where none of it was happening. He also started to dwell on how he used to be before the event—a boy who didn’t flinch at loud voices, who didn’t scan every room for danger. That boy felt impossibly distant.

At work, Samir learned to avoid any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation. He never spoke up when a foreman gave unfair orders, and he ate lunch alone rather than risk a debate about sports or politics. When a police car appeared on site during a routine safety inspection, Samir felt his stomach drop and his palms go slick with sweat. His physical reactions were immediate and overpowering—his heart hammering, his breath shallow—and in that moment the memory of his father’s heavy footsteps on the stairs would lock into place, as clear as a photograph. He had come to believe that authority figures carried the same threat his father had, that their presence meant something bad was about to happen.

Samir began studying people’s faces and body language constantly, trying to detect if they were a threat. He would watch a coworker’s jaw tighten and assume an argument was coming, even when the man was just concentrating. When a delivery of lumber took longer than expected, Samir was certain that something bad was happening—maybe a fight had broken out, maybe someone was hurt. This threat monitoring only made the memories more accessible; the more he watched for danger, the more his mind supplied him with images of his father’s rage. And those images, in turn, made him avoid people even more. He stopped going to family gatherings. He told himself he was fine alone.

Over time, a cycle tightened. A trigger—a raised voice, a police car, a question about his plans for next year—would bring the memory rushing in. The memory would spike his physical reactivity and his scanning for threat. That threat state would drive him deeper into fantasy escape and past dwelling. And those maladaptive strategies, in turn, made the triggers feel more frequent and more dangerous, because he was never present enough to test whether a situation was actually safe. Talking about the future became especially unbearable; when a friend asked what he wanted to do next year, Samir felt a cold dread and saw his mother’s face in the doorway, and he changed the subject.

Now, at 41, Samir has come to therapy because he can no longer function at work. He was written up for failing to respond to a foreman’s instruction—he had been so lost in a daydream that he didn’t hear the man calling his name. What frightens him most is the feeling that he is losing his grip on the present entirely, that he is living more and more inside those old photographs. He hopes, quietly, that someone can help him find a way back to the person he was before, though he is not sure that person exists anymore.
